title: Moral certainty excluding fear rejected by most Romans as clashing with Trent’s ‘may fear’
source_text: XX. Verum haec sententia quae statuit homines justos, saltem perfectiores, habere posse de propria gratia atque justitia certitudinem, non quidem fidei, sed moralem, quae omnem non modo dubitationem, sed formidinem etiam excludat, hodie a maxima parte Theologorum Scholae Romanae rejicitur; idque quoniam ipsis non videtur satis congruere cum Tridentini Synodi decreto. Haec enim sunt verba istius Synodi, Sess. 6. cap. 9. Nam sicut nemo pius de Dei misericordia, de Christi merito, deque Sacramentorum virtute & efficacia dubitare debet; sic quilibet dum seipsum, suamque propriam infirmitatem, & indispositionem respicit, de sua gratia formidare & timere potest: cum nullus scire valeat certitudine fidei, cui non potest subesse falsum, se gratiam Dei esse consecutum. Ubi cum Concilium decernat quemlibet justum de sua gratia formidare & timere posse, planum est, ex ejus mente, fideles in hac vita non posse pervenire ad eam de propria gratia certitudinem, quae omnem formidinem & timorem ex iis, hac in parte, expellat.
pass_a_gloss: But this opinion which holds that just persons, at least the more perfect, can have concerning their own grace and righteousness a certainty—not indeed of faith, but moral—which excludes not only every doubt but even fear, is today rejected by the greatest part of the theologians of the Roman School; and that because it does not seem to them to agree sufficiently with the decree of the Tridentine Synod. For these are the words of that Synod, Session 6, chapter 9: For just as no pious person ought to doubt of God’s mercy, of Christ’s merit, and of the virtue and efficacy of the sacraments; so anyone, while he looks at himself and his own infirmity and indisposition, can fear and dread concerning his grace: since no one can know with the certainty of faith, to which falsehood cannot be subject, that he has obtained the grace of God. Where, since the Council decrees that any just person can fear and dread concerning his grace, it is plain that, in its mind, the faithful in this life cannot arrive at that certainty concerning their own grace which drives out from them, in this matter, every fear and dread.
pass_b_english: Most Roman theologians now reject fear-excluding moral certainty of grace.
Trent’s ‘anyone may fear regarding his grace’ is taken to bar certainty that banishes all fear.
